title: The War Within the War: How the Croat-Bosniak Alliance Collapsed
sources: Balkan Battlegrounds Vol. I, ch. 39, pp. 219 and 225, Croat-Bosniak fighting chronology
ICTY Prlic et al. Trial Judgment (IT-04-74-T), Herceg-Bosna/HVO joint-criminal-enterprise findings
ICTY Kordic and Cerkez Trial Judgment (IT-95-14/2-T), Lasva Valley attack findings
ICTY Hadzihasanovic and Kubura Trial Judgment (IT-01-47-T), superior-responsibility findings for discrete ARBiH crimes
source_note: Balkan Battlegrounds anchors the transition from local clashes to open fighting. The ICTY judgments support separate actor-specific legal findings: Prlic and Kordic/Cerkez address the Herceg-Bosna/HVO campaign, while Hadzihasanovic/Kubura addresses narrower superior responsibility findings for discrete crimes by ARBiH subordinates. The essay does not collapse those findings into equivalent culpability and reproduces no source prose.
content:
During 1992, HVO and ARBiH formations cooperated against the VRS in several theatres, but their relationship varied sharply by locality. Balkan Battlegrounds records clashes at Prozor in October 1992 and Gornji Vakuf in January 1993 before fighting widened across central Bosnia and Herzegovina from mid-January 1993. The result was a second active front for the Bosnian government and the collapse of the wartime alliance in the affected areas.

The political and military projects behind that fighting were not legally interchangeable. The ICTY Prlic et al. Trial Judgment (IT-04-74-T) found that leaders of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna and the HVO participated in a joint criminal enterprise directed at removing the Bosnian Muslim population from territories claimed for a Croat entity. That finding addressed the common criminal purpose, the institutions used to pursue it, and Croatia's involvement in the project.

For central Bosnia, the ICTY Kordic and Cerkez Trial Judgment (IT-95-14/2-T) found that HVO attacks on Bosniak civilians and villages in the Lasva Valley were organized through political and military structures rather than being spontaneous communal violence. The judgment attributed responsibility to named Bosnian Croat political and military actors for specific attacks and persecutions.

The ICTY Hadzihasanovic and Kubura Trial Judgment (IT-01-47-T) addressed crimes committed by members of ARBiH formations against Croat and Serb victims. Its superior responsibility findings concerned failures by particular ARBiH commanders to prevent or punish discrete crimes by subordinates. Those findings record ARBiH culpability without converting a narrower command-responsibility case into a finding of an equivalent territorial campaign.

Operationally, ARBiH formations that had faced the VRS now also fought HVO forces in central Bosnia and Herzegovina, while HVO formations defended and expanded positions linked to Herceg-Bosna's territorial project. The fighting continued until the Washington Agreement of March 1994 ended the Croat-Bosniak war and established the Federation framework. The record is therefore one of a broken alliance, distinct campaigns and crimes, and separately adjudicated responsibility.
